title: How Senior Engineers Actually Use Coding Agents
objective: Describe the workflow pattern experienced engineers use with agentic coding tools (Claude Code, Codex, etc.), and explain why each practice exists.

content_blocks.heading: Not "Vibe Coding"
content_blocks.body:
The engineers getting real value from coding agents aren't 'vibe coding' — typing a vague prompt like 'add a login page' and accepting whatever comes back without reading it closely. That pattern produces code that looks plausible, passes a quick visual check, and then breaks in a way nobody can explain three weeks later, because nobody actually understood what the agent did or why.

The alternative isn't typing more carefully. It's structuring the whole interaction so the agent's work gets checked cheaply and often, by something more reliable than a glance. Across Anthropic's own best-practice guidance and independent practitioner write-ups — people solving real production problems, not demoing a feature for an audience — the same five habits show up over and over. None of them require a different model or a fancier tool. They're about how the work gets organized.

content_blocks.heading: 1. Separate Planning from Implementation
content_blocks.body:
Before any code gets written, the agent explores the codebase and proposes a plan: which files it intends to touch, what the implementation approach is, and what could realistically go wrong. Only after a human reviews that plan does implementation start.

What this looks like in practice: ask an agent to 'add rate limiting to the login endpoint,' and a good plan comes back looking something like:
- Files: `auth/routes.py` (add decorator), `auth/rate_limiter.py` (new), `tests/test_rate_limiter.py` (new)
- Approach: token-bucket limiter backed by Redis, keyed by IP + username
- Risk: the Redis instance already handles session storage — need to confirm a new key namespace won't collide, and check whether Redis is even available in the test environment

That risk note is the whole point. If the agent had just started implementing, it might have silently assumed Redis was available everywhere, written code that passes locally, and broken CI the moment it was actually depended on — or collided with existing session keys in production. Catching that assumption in a one-paragraph plan costs thirty seconds of review. Catching it after the code is written, reviewed, and merged costs an incident.

Skipping this step is the single biggest cause of an agent confidently solving the wrong problem — not because the agent is unreliable, but because an unreviewed first guess about scope is exactly as likely to be wrong as a human's unreviewed first guess, and agents commit to that first guess faster than people do.

exercises.prompt: An agent is about to implement a feature that touches five files in an unfamiliar part of the codebase. What's the highest-leverage thing to do before it writes any code?

options: Let it start implementing immediately so you can review the diff when it's done
Have it propose a plan first (files, approach, risks) and review that before starting
Write the code yourself instead of delegating it, since the codebase is unfamiliar
Ask it to run all five file changes in parallel subagents to save time
definition.explanation: Separating planning from implementation is the single highest-leverage practice — it catches 'solving the wrong problem' while it's still cheap to redirect, before any code exists to un-write.

exercises.prompt: In the rate-limiting example, the agent's plan flagged a Redis key-collision risk before writing any code. What would have happened if that risk had NOT been caught until after the code was merged?

options: Code review would have caught it instead, at roughly the same cost
The bug would ship and get discovered as a production incident instead
The test suite would catch the key collision automatically before merge
The agent would refuse to proceed without resolving the ambiguity first
definition.explanation: The value of catching a risk during planning is timing — the same flaw can exist either way, but catching it before code exists costs a sentence of review, while catching it after merge costs an incident response.

content_blocks.heading: 2. Repository Context Files Do the Onboarding
content_blocks.body:
CLAUDE.md (and Codex's AGENTS.md) encode the things a new hire would otherwise take weeks to absorb by osmosis: which commands actually run the test suite, which directories are off-limits, what the team's naming conventions are, which parts of the codebase are legacy and shouldn't be touched without a specific reason.

Without this, every new session re-derives all of it from scratch — by guessing, by grepping around, or by trying the wrong test command and failing before trying the right one. That's not just slower; a wrong guess about a boundary (editing something in `legacy/` because nothing said not to) is exactly the kind of mistake a plan-review step might not catch, because the resulting code can still look entirely reasonable.

The two examples below show the range: a minimal file that states only what an agent couldn't discover by reading the code, and a fuller one from a similarly-shaped project that also encodes house style, architectural boundaries, and agent-behavior rules end to end.

examples.label: Minimal CLAUDE.md
examples.content:
## Commands
- Tests: `make test` (not `pytest` directly — it sets required env vars)
- Lint: `make lint`
- Dev server: `make dev` (binds to :8000)

## Boundaries
- `legacy/` is frozen — report bugs there, don't fix them
- Migrations go through `alembic revision --autogenerate`, never hand-written SQL

examples.label: A fuller CLAUDE.md, from a similarly-shaped project
examples.content:
# CLAUDE.md

## 1. Project Overview

This repository contains a full-stack learning platform for
software engineering and technical leadership.

Users can:
- Study structured software engineering topics
- Complete coding exercises and quizzes
- Track learning progress
- Work through timed Pomodoro learning sessions

### Architecture

- Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS
- Backend: Python, Flask, SQLAlchemy
- Database: PostgreSQL
- Infrastructure: Docker, AWS
- Testing: Vitest, React Testing Library, pytest

The frontend communicates with the backend through REST APIs.

## 2. Repository Structure

```text
/
├── frontend/
│   ├── src/app/          # Next.js routes
│   ├── src/components/   # Reusable UI components
│   ├── src/hooks/        # Custom React hooks
│   ├── src/lib/          # API clients and utilities
│   └── src/types/        # Shared frontend types
├── backend/
│   ├── app/api/          # Flask API endpoints
│   ├── app/models/       # SQLAlchemy models
│   ├── app/services/     # Business logic
│   ├── migrations/       # Alembic migrations
│   └── tests/            # Backend tests
├── docs/                 # Architecture and design docs
├── docker-compose.yml
└── CLAUDE.md
```

## 3. Development Commands

Run these from the repository root unless noted.

### Setup
- `make setup` — Install dependencies
- `make dev` — Start frontend, backend and database
- `make down` — Stop services

### Testing
- `make test` — Run all tests
- `make test-frontend` — Frontend unit tests
- `make test-backend` — Backend tests

### Quality
- `make lint` — Run linters
- `make typecheck` — TypeScript checks
- `make format` — Format code

Always prefer these commands over invoking underlying
tools directly. They configure required environment variables.

## 4. Coding Standards

### General
- Prefer simple, readable solutions.
- Avoid premature abstraction.
- Follow existing conventions before introducing new ones.
- Do not add dependencies without explaining why.
- Do not refactor unrelated code.

### Frontend
- Use TypeScript strict mode.
- Prefer React Server Components by default.
- Use Client Components only when interactivity requires them.
- Use functional components and hooks.
- Keep API requests outside presentation components.
- Avoid `any` unless explicitly justified.

### Backend
- Use Python type hints.
- Keep Flask route handlers thin.
- Business logic belongs in `services/`.
- Database access belongs in models or repository modules.
- Validate incoming requests.
- Return consistent API error responses.

### Naming
- React components: PascalCase
- Hooks: useCamelCase
- TypeScript functions: camelCase
- Python functions: snake_case
- Constants: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE

## 5. Architectural Boundaries

These rules are mandatory.

### Frontend
- Components must not access the database directly.
- API calls must go through the shared API client.
- Do not place business logic in UI components.

### Backend
- Routes must not contain complex business logic.
- Services must not depend on Flask request objects.
- Database schema changes require Alembic migrations.

### Protected Areas
- Do not edit `legacy/` without explicit permission.
- Do not modify production infrastructure configuration
  unless specifically requested.
- Never commit `.env` files, credentials, or API keys.
- Never modify existing migrations that have been applied.

## 6. Working With Existing Code

Before implementing a feature:

1. Inspect relevant files and existing patterns.
2. Identify the smallest reasonable change.
3. Check whether reusable implementations already exist.
4. Explain architectural trade-offs when applicable.
5. Implement the change.
6. Run relevant tests and quality checks.
7. Summarize the changes and any remaining risks.

Do not create duplicate utilities or abstractions.

## 7. Testing Expectations

Every new feature should include appropriate tests.

### Frontend
- Test user-visible behavior.
- Prefer React Testing Library.
- Avoid testing implementation details.

### Backend
- Test service logic independently.
- Test API response codes and validation.
- Mock external services where appropriate.

For bug fixes, add a regression test when practical.

Never claim tests passed unless they were actually executed.

## 8. Database Rules

- Use SQLAlchemy models.
- All schema changes require Alembic migrations.
- Never manually modify production database schemas.
- Avoid N+1 queries.
- Add indexes when justified by query patterns.

Always inspect existing migrations before creating new ones.

## 9. Security Requirements

- Never log secrets or authentication tokens.
- Validate all untrusted inputs.
- Enforce authorization on backend endpoints.
- Do not trust client-provided user IDs.
- Never expose internal stack traces to API consumers.

## 10. AI Agent Behavior

### Before Coding
For changes affecting multiple components or services:
- Present a concise implementation plan.
- Identify relevant files.
- Explain important trade-offs.

For trivial changes, proceed directly.

### During Coding
- Make incremental, focused changes.
- Preserve backwards compatibility unless instructed.
- Avoid introducing unnecessary dependencies.
- Do not silently change public APIs.

### After Coding
Provide a summary containing:
1. What changed
2. Files modified
3. Tests executed and their results
4. Known limitations
5. Suggested next steps, if applicable

### When Uncertain
Do not invent assumptions about business requirements.
Inspect documentation or ask for clarification when a
decision could materially affect functionality.

## 11. Definition of Done

A task is complete when:
- The requested behavior is implemented.
- Relevant tests pass.
- Type checking and linting pass where applicable.
- New behavior is documented when necessary.
- No unrelated files were modified.
- Known risks are communicated.

If checks cannot run, explain why.

exercises.prompt: A CLAUDE.md says: "Tests: `make test` (not `pytest` directly — it sets required env vars)." An agent ignores this and runs `pytest` directly. What's the most likely result?

options: The tests pass normally since pytest and make test run identical code
Tests fail or behave incorrectly because required environment variables are missing
Make test gets triggered automatically as a fallback when pytest runs
CLAUDE.md instructions are suggestions only and have no effect on behavior
definition.explanation: This is exactly why the instruction exists — `make test` does something `pytest` alone doesn't (setting required env vars), so skipping it isn't a stylistic choice, it changes whether the tests run correctly at all.

content_blocks.heading: 3. Give the Agent a Check It Can Run on Itself
content_blocks.body:
The highest-leverage habit is making sure the agent has a fast, reliable way to verify its own work — a test suite, a type checker, a build — before a human ever looks at it. This is why 'write a failing test first, then make it pass' works so well with agents specifically: the check is unambiguous, and the agent can iterate against it alone, dozens of times if needed, without spending any of a reviewer's attention.

Concretely: instead of 'fix the bug where discount codes don't stack,' a more effective instruction is 'write a test that applies two discount codes and asserts the combined total is correct — it should currently fail — then make it pass.' The agent now has a mechanical, binary signal (red → green) instead of a vague goal, and it can run that test as many times as it needs. Compare that to an agent asked only to 'fix it,' with no test: its only way to know it's done is to re-read its own code and declare victory — precisely the failure mode that erodes trust over time.

The same idea extends past tests: a type checker catches whole categories of mistakes (wrong argument types, null-handling gaps) in seconds, and a build that fails loudly is better than one that silently produces a broken artifact. Whatever the check is, the property that matters is the same: fast, unambiguous, and runnable by the agent without waiting on a human.

exercises.prompt: Which instruction gives an agent fixing a bug the clearest, most unambiguous way to know when it's actually done?

options: Fix the bug where discount codes fail to stack together properly
Investigate the discount code logic and make any necessary improvements
Write a failing test for stacked codes, then make it pass
Review the discount code function and clean up unclear parts
definition.explanation: Only this option gives the agent a mechanical, binary signal — a test that goes from red to green — rather than a goal it has to judge as 'done' using its own self-assessment.

content_blocks.heading: 4. Delegation for Independent, Parallelizable Work
content_blocks.body:
Senior engineers increasingly run multiple agents on genuinely independent sub-tasks — one agent researching how an unfamiliar library's API works while another implements a feature that doesn't depend on that research yet, or one agent per independent microservice — rather than one agent doing everything serially.

The test for whether a task is actually parallelizable is simple, and easy to get wrong under time pressure: would two humans working on these two pieces need to talk to each other before either could finish? If yes, it's not independent — it's sequential work wearing a parallel disguise. Splitting 'rename this widely-used function' and 'add a new endpoint that calls it' across two agents looks like parallelism, but the rename agent will finish, the endpoint agent will call the function under its old name, and now there's a merge conflict and a broken build to untangle — the coordination cost of fixing it typically exceeds whatever time was saved running the two agents at once.

Genuinely independent work looks more like: one agent adds tests to code that already works and isn't changing, while another builds an unrelated feature in a different part of the codebase. Neither needs information from the other to finish.

exercises.prompt: Which pair of tasks is safe to delegate to two agents running in parallel?

options: Renaming a shared utility function, and updating every file that calls it
Adding tests to stable code, and building an unrelated new feature
Writing an API endpoint, and writing the client code that calls it
Refactoring a shared config file, and adding a feature that reads it
definition.explanation: The other three pairs all have one agent's output depend on the other's — a rename affects every caller, an endpoint's shape determines the client code, and a config refactor changes what a feature reading it expects. Only this pair is genuinely independent.

content_blocks.heading: 5. The Engineer Stays the Reviewer
content_blocks.body:
None of the above changes who's responsible for correctness. The role shifts from 'typing every line' to 'directing, reviewing, and signing off' — which is a familiar shape, not a new one: it's close to how a staff engineer already works with a junior engineer's pull requests, just compressed from a day's turnaround to minutes, and repeatable across far more concurrent work than one person could mentor directly.

That similarity is also the warning. The same review discipline that catches a junior engineer's subtle mistakes — reading the diff, not just the description; checking the edge cases; asking 'what happens if this input is empty or huge' — has to apply here too, and it's tempting to skip it specifically because the output looks polished and confident. An agent's code reads as fluently as a senior engineer's even when it's subtly wrong, which is a different failure mode than a junior engineer's code, which usually *looks* uncertain exactly where it is uncertain.

exercises.prompt: Why is reviewing an agent's code arguably harder than reviewing a junior engineer's code, even though the agent's code often looks more polished?

options: Agent code is always functionally correct, so review is just a formality
Confident, fluent code can be subtly wrong without looking uncertain at all
Agents refuse to submit code that hasn't already been fully tested
Junior engineers write code that is harder to read than agent output
definition.explanation: A junior engineer's uncertainty often shows in the code itself — hedgy comments, obvious gaps. An agent's output reads fluently regardless of whether it's actually correct, which removes a cue reviewers normally rely on.

content_blocks.heading: The Bottom Line
content_blocks.body:
None of this is about typing faster. It's about structuring the interaction so an agent's mistakes get caught cheaply — by a test, a build, a plan review — instead of expensively, in production or after hours of work built on a wrong assumption.

Every practice in this lesson is really the same idea applied at a different point in the workflow: plans catch scope mistakes before code exists; tests catch logic mistakes before a human looks; context files catch 'didn't know the rule' mistakes before they happen at all; delegation boundaries catch coordination mistakes before they become merge conflicts; and review catches everything that slipped through the earlier gates.
